title: The Craziest Things Napoleon Did

beats.say: March 1815. A narrow road in the French Alps. A wall of French soldiers blocks the way, muskets ready.
Their orders from the king: stop one man. Napoleon Bonaparte, the former emperor of France, who has just escaped from exile.
And Napoleon does the craziest thing possible. He walks straight toward the guns.
Wait. Is that... him?
Soldiers! Don't you recognize me?
Hold that thought. We'll see how it ends at number one.
Because this man did a lot of crazy things. Today: the seven craziest things Napoleon ever did. One of them involves rabbits.
Number seven: before he ruled France, Napoleon wanted to be... a writer.
In 1795 he was a broke young army officer with a lot of feelings. He was engaged to Désirée Clary, the daughter of a rich merchant family from Marseille.
So he wrote a short romance called Clisson and Eugénie. The hero, Clisson, is a brilliant young soldier. Sound like anyone?
Clisson is a war hero who's tired of fighting and dreams of a quiet life in the countryside. Very subtle, Napoleon.
Clisson marries the lovely Eugénie, then goes back to war. While he's away, she falls for his friend. Heartbroken, Clisson dies in battle.
Meanwhile, in real life, Napoleon dumped Désirée for a stylish widow named Joséphine. He never finished the book.
The pages were later scattered and sold off. Scholars only pieced the full story back together in 2007.
And Désirée? She married another French general, Jean Bernadotte. He later became King of Sweden. So the girl Napoleon dumped became a queen.
Number six comes with a warning label: it might not be totally true.
It's July 1807. Napoleon has just made peace with Russia at a town called Tilsit, near the Baltic Sea.
He had first met the Russian tsar on a fancy raft, floating in the middle of a river, to talk peace.
To celebrate, his chief of staff, Marshal Berthier, set up a rabbit hunt for him on his estate near Paris.
Your Majesty, I've got hundreds of rabbits ready for you!
Splendid. Let them go!
The problem? Berthier's men had bought tame rabbits from farmers. And tame rabbits think people mean dinner.
So instead of running away, a horde of rabbits charged straight at Napoleon.
In the story, they swarmed around his legs, and the conqueror of Europe retreated to his carriage.
This tale comes from the memoirs of General Thiébault, a French officer who didn't like Berthier. So take it with a pinch of salt.
Number five: Napoleon versus the robot.
In 1809, Napoleon captured Vienna, the capital of Austria, and moved into its emperor's summer palace.
There, a showman named Johann Mälzel showed him one of the most famous machines in Europe: the Mechanical Turk.
It was a life-sized figure in a turban, sitting at a wooden cabinet with a chessboard. And it beat almost everyone.
Your Majesty, care for a game?
Against a machine? This will be easy.
Accounts say Napoleon tested it by making an illegal move. The Turk calmly put the piece back.
He kept cheating. Finally, the Turk swept every piece off the board.
The story goes that Napoleon was amused, played properly, and lost anyway.
The twist? It wasn't a robot. A human chess master was hiding inside the cabinet.
So the man who conquered half of Europe lost at chess to a guy in a box.
The Turk kept fooling crowds for decades, until it burned in a museum fire in Philadelphia in 1854.

show.title: He Brought Scientists to a War

beats.say: Number four: in 1798, Napoleon invaded Egypt. Egypt was rich, officially part of the Ottoman Empire, and on Britain's route to India.
He brought tens of thousands of soldiers. And something armies don't usually pack: about one hundred and sixty-seven scholars.

show.label: Scholars who went with Napoleon's army to Egypt

beats.say: Mathematicians, chemists, doctors, artists, even a musician. One of their leaders was Gaspard Monge, a famous mathematician.
General, we'll measure every pyramid in Egypt!
Wonderful. Just stay behind the soldiers.
While the army fought, the scholars measured temples, drew maps, and collected animals and plants.
In Cairo, Napoleon even set up a science club, the Institute of Egypt.
Their notes became a giant set of books called the Description of Egypt, and set off a craze for all things Egyptian across Europe.
Then, in July 1799, French soldiers fixing an old fort near the town of Rosetta dug up a broken stone covered in writing.
It became the Rosetta Stone, the key that later helped experts read hieroglyphs.
But here's the crazy part. The British navy had already destroyed most of Napoleon's fleet. His army was stuck.
So in August 1799, Napoleon quietly sailed home, and left his army behind.
In 1801, his stranded troops surrendered, and the British took the stone. It's still in the British Museum in London.
Number three. By 1809, Napoleon was emperor, and he wanted a son to take over one day. Joséphine hadn't given him one, so he divorced her.
His new bride was Marie-Louise, the eighteen-year-old daughter of the Emperor of Austria. Napoleon had beaten her father's armies again and again.
Fun family fact: she was also the great-niece of Marie Antoinette, the French queen executed during the Revolution.
And Napoleon didn't go to the wedding. It was held in Vienna by proxy, which means someone else stood in for the groom.
The stand-in was Archduke Charles, an Austrian general who had beaten Napoleon in a battle the year before.
So... where exactly is my husband?
Busy. You're stuck with me today.
Then Marie-Louise rode to France. Napoleon was so impatient, he raced out to meet her carriage on the road.
A year later they had a son, and Napoleon gave the baby a title: King of Rome.
Number two is less funny, but it might be the craziest of all.
Before Napoleon, France was a messy patchwork of local laws. The rules could change from one region to the next.
So in 1804, he gave France one clear rulebook: the Civil Code, later called the Napoleonic Code.

show.label: Articles in Napoleon's Civil Code of 1804
show.sub: one rulebook for the whole country

beats.say: It said every man was equal before the law, no matter who his parents were. Though, to be fair, it gave women far fewer rights than men.
His armies carried it across Europe, and it stuck, even after he was gone.
Its ideas shaped the laws of many countries, from Belgium to Chile, and even Louisiana and Quebec.
Years later, in exile, Napoleon said this was his real legacy.

show.text: My true glory is not to have won forty battles... What nothing will destroy, what will live forever, is my Civil Code.
show.who: Napoleon, in exile on Saint Helena (as reported by his companions)

show.title: He Took Back France with One Sentence

beats.say: And number one. In 1814, Napoleon finally lost. His enemies captured Paris, and he had to give up his throne.
They sent him to rule Elba, a small island off the coast of Italy. It's only about four times the size of Manhattan.
They even let him keep the title of emperor. Emperor... of a small island.
He took the job seriously. He designed Elba a flag with three golden bees, built roads, and reorganized the island's iron mines.
He had a tiny army, a tiny navy, and his mother moved in to keep him company.
But he was bored. And he heard the new king of France, Louis the Eighteenth, was not very popular.
Pack the ships. We're going to Paris.
After about ten months on Elba, he slipped away with around a thousand men, and landed in southern France.
He marched north on mountain roads through the Alps, to avoid towns loyal to the king.
And that brings us back to Laffrey, and that wall of soldiers sent to stop him.
According to accounts of the day, he stepped forward and said:

show.text: Soldiers of the Fifth, I am your emperor. If there is one among you who wants to kill his emperor, here I am.
show.who: Napoleon at Laffrey, 7 March 1815 (as reported; wording varies)

beats.say: Nobody fired. Instead, the soldiers broke ranks and ran to him.
Long live the Emperor!
More and more troops joined him along the way. Less than two weeks later, he was back in Paris, and the king had fled.
He had taken back a whole country without fighting a single battle.
It didn't last. About three months later, he lost the Battle of Waterloo, in what's now Belgium.
This time, the British sent him to Saint Helena, a tiny island in the middle of the South Atlantic. He died there in 1821.
So that's Napoleon: a romance writer, a rabbit victim, a chess cheat, a science fan, a no-show groom, a lawmaker, and a man who stopped an army with one sentence.
Which one was the craziest? Tell us in the comments.

description:
Napoleon Bonaparte wrote a romance novel, (maybe) got chased by rabbits, cheated at chess against a fake robot, took about 167 scholars to a war, skipped his own wedding, rewrote France's laws, and took back a whole country with one sentence. Here are the seven craziest things he did, counted down from seven to one, with the legend clearly flagged. Chapters are added automatically.
